Don’t know what’s up with all these removed comments. Anyway, I rewatched it when it was in theaters over the summer for the first time since like high school and I really didn’t like it either. Heath Ledger was like the only decent part. I didn’t like any of the characters or the writing. Felt so stale and just cartoonish. Just a boring movie for me

>I never understood why is it said to be one of the greatest movie. 

Because hyperbole exists.

Part of why it was so well received has to do with how the filmmakers chose to reinterprete such a loved character for cinema. While it's not a complete revamp reinterpretation, it still allowed the movie theatre audiences to view Batman from a new perspective many had never considered.

The fact that it was a continuation of a very well recieved movie and included what would go on to be an iconic performance helped obviously. But Batman was generally perceived as a silly comic book by people who never actually read the comics. The Dark Knight allowed a wider audience to see what people like Denny O'Neil and Neal Adams or even Frank Miller had been doing decades before.

Batman has a long history, and it's easy for an audience to hyperfixate on one era and believe that's the only way to view the character or the world of Gotham. The Dark Knight and the trilogy as a whole really opened up that history and layered it throughout the three movies in a very subtle way that most probably don't even catch the little references and how they apply to the themes of the movies. 

The Dark Knight is this approach at its peak.

You don't find it believable that Wayne would feel bad about the fact that the love of his life and the man he was relying on to allow him to give up the Batman mantle (the man Wayne thought was Gotham's true hero) are killed and disfigured? His whole point in taking on Batman as a persona was to prevent those kinds of things from happening. I don't know what to tell you if you can't grasp that basic character development. 

I don't have any problem with a claim that the movie is overrated. I LOVED it when it came out, but over the years some of its flaws have become more and more apparent to me. But some of these gripes are a little bit bizarre IMHO.

To a lot of your points, I think what you're missing is that Batman is just a vigilante. The choices he makes aren't inherently for the greater good just because he's a super hero. The point is that Batman imposes his will as he sees fit, and the Joker spends the film antagonizing that idea. The Batman might not deserve all the power he gives himself.

If you think of the average cinema fan they are mostly spending their time and money seeing the mega-budget blockbuster movies. Anecdotally, I've heard it too many times that people only want to watch films in the cinema that require a cinema; the big loud action movies. 

When you compare mega-budget movies, which I'm defining as movies that cost more then $100 million to make, then The Dark Knight isn't overrated at all. In this category it is one of the best. Also, when you compare it to other superhero/comicbook movies it is not overrated. 

Rating by what it is, a mega-budget movie, then it is a solid 4-4.5 stars. But comparing it to all movies I don't think it would be in my top 100, probably not my top 250.

Why so serious? My problem with the film is it’s going for a realistic gangster drama but the plot is too inherently silly to be taken seriously.  I mentioned this to a friend and they said it’s just a comic book movie it’s not The Godfather.  Exactly.  I think it’s poorly written but I do think Heath Ledger and some of Nolan’s visuals keep the film entertaining for the most part but the best comic book adaptations are the ones that lean into the humor and silly concepts.  Superman I & II, Batman and Batman Returns, Spider-Man I & II, and Iron Man work better for this reason.

>The fact that he never kills, just to prove that hes not a villian is just idiotic. 

That's not why he doesn't kill. He doesn't kill because he knows that Batman as a symbol, (his stated goal in Begins), doesn't work if he's a symbol of extreme vigilantism. 

>Are you telling me that because he pushed Harvey to fight crime and eventually Harvey got burnt makes Batman feel bad?

He feels bad because Harvey was what Bruce had been trying to achieve. A world that doesn't need Batman because it has someone who will be able to protect Gotham without breaking the rules the way he does. He believed in Harvey. That's why he got so mad when he found Harvey threatening one of Joker's goons.

Honestly a lot of your gripes here are actually misreading what's actually happening in the film.

Its the story of good vs evil.

Joker uses batman rule against him of not killing. Pushes him to the limit. When he could not but he turns harvey dent evil.

Just because Harvey dent has turned evil doesn't mean city should loose hop with him.

So batman choses to sacrifice himself to save the hero of the city. Through out the story we seee countless times jokwr win with him not caring. But in his last gambit he lost because batman cares.

Joker can do as much evil as he could but he never could sacrifice. That is where batman beat him.

> The fact that he never kills, just to prove that hes not a villian is just idiotic

If it helps, the emotional climax of the Dark Knight follows Batman deciding to kill Harvey Dent to prevent Dent from murdering Jim Gordon in front of his family - Batman breaks his rule to spare another child from experiencing what he experienced.

It's like poetry. It rhymes.

> Is it really better than the first Batman, Spiderman 2 or X-men 2 or Thor?

It really is.

as with every nolan film, multiple viewings make the flaws in his craft glaringly obvious. mainly, his inability to "show, don't tell". the dude has characters explain the mechanics of his scripts so thoroughly that it's actually funny after the first watch.

The not kill complaint is bizarre in this context. I think Batman's stated mantra of not killing people is a silly comic book convention, but I also think it's absurd to tell the character of Bruce Wayne that he should just be going around murdering people. He's just taken on the Batman mantle at this point and the Joker is a brand new threat. In the comic book runs where Batman has been fighting Joker for decades and Joker has killed thousands of people then yeah, I kind of question Batman's belief that not killing the Joker is the morally correct choice. But in this movie? Killing another human being isn't something that's just like ordering Uber Eats- thinking that Bruce Wayne would immediately decide to murder someone rather than uphold his principles is just a very silly complaint to throw at the movie and character.

The political themes were very timely and something people weren't used to getting in movies. Seeing the Joker's terrorism and the societal effects it had, and seeing Harvey Dent becoming a monster as he became frustrated with the failures of the system were both relatable. Plus the way Batman used his version of the Patriot Act while rejecting it as a permanent solution was an inspiring criticism of what the US was doing. Those themes continue to be relevant today and were vital context for what made people do passionate about it.

Hey..

I'm not quarreling with you.

But what I am going to say is that it's the "Rebel without a cause" of our generation.(James Dean's tragic accident  predates that movie)

That is to say it's an above average film that has taken on legendary status hugely because of the focus on Ledger's performance above plot or even character development.  

So I think it's impossible in terms of reception to separate the overall film from the post Ledger hype by fans.  

So to me the most frustrating thing isn't so much the fanbase, but rather Cinema blogs, YouTube channels, and magazines bending over backwards to include The Dark Knight as part of a quota so that fans don't raise a storm.

A case in point is Cinefix (which usually an excellent source for movie content) is making the scene where the Joker dangles upside down the best shot in all Cinema (and with lists of the runners up)

Beating out..

Darth Vader standing over the corpses of the dead rebellion.

The door closing in the Searchers.

The lone hero in the smoke (Yojimbo)

A certain rebirth in Vertigo

Charles Kane standing in a wrecked room (which has been echoed in the Conversation and Batman returns) 

.
I don't want to seem too dismissive..

But I feel like pre-Dark Knight, to be considered a masterpiece, a film would have to be an amazing dramatic and aesthetic experience.

Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings trilogy comes to mind.

Now I feel like it's kind of a self-burning bridge.

The Dark Knight can be appreciated for a singular performance, but don't you dare do the same with The amazing Spider-Man!


So where I'm trying to go with this is that discourse whether positive or negative is almost treated with soft gloves-- where saying something negative is like criticizing The Joker himself, or saying something positive is a bit of a debt to society.

My big issue with all the Nolan Batman movies (and most Nolan films overall) is that they aren't emotionally affecting. Good acting, well staged set pieces, well shot and paced, and I just don't friggin care about any of it. People live and die and I don't care. It's like every criticism made of Kubrick during his lifetime, technically brilliant and emotionally distant, and treated as a manifesto rather than a flaw. Nolan is Kubrick without the wit or quirk. 

TDK is good. But it isn't as good as The Batman, itself a flawed movie that at least has some emotional resonance to it. I'd love for one of these pseudo film noir movies to embrace not just the style and the darkness but also the melodrama. 

That said I loved Oppenheimer, Nolan isn't all bad, but TDK is not as good as it's fans say Imho

Doubling back: Batman is totally unprepared by Nolan’s Joker, who’s goal is to expose Gotham’s morality as a sham.

To accomplish this, the Joker succeeds in destroying Gotham’s police force, judicial system, and social infrastructure (his boat experiment only fails because Tiny Lister’s character - who has no relationship with anyone else in the film - is a good guy). Joker’s last move is to break Harvey Dent, which breaks Batman, who colludes with Gordon to rebuild Gotham on a lie, which means that the Joker wins. 

So the film matters because 1) it picks at the loathsome politics of the Bush administration (which gave rise to Trump - who is a Jokerish figure), 2) it anticipated the cinematic advent of superheroics-as-fascism which were heralded by the release of the first Iron Man movie ~2 months before, 3) it’s themes defined subsequent cinematic Batmen (Affleck’s Batman is a hero who has “lived long enough to become a villain” when we meet him in Batman vs Superman. Reeves’ Batman is an attempt to reconstruct the Batman mythos using the iconography and plot elements of Nolan’s movie), and because 4) ir left and indelible mark on subsequent blockbusters (Skyfall and Mission Impossible 5/6 owe an enormous narrative/stylistic debt to Nolan’s work, here).

Coming back to your argument. We don’t have to like or admire any of this, but we do have acknowledge it if we want to understand it.

This actually sounds like a right answer, for lack of a better term.

The tone is like a mid budget crime drama, but it occupies a world of special effects action fantasies.

When folks are comparing The Dark Knight to a movie, isn't something like Goodfellas or Heat, it's something like X-Men or the Raimi Spider-Man movies, or The Avengers years later.

If what is at play is crime drama structure and ideas, then maybe Nolan's accomplishment is making a huge budget crime drama with superhero elements. 

I don't consider that to be a negative thing, but i also feel like it makes people who are subconscious crime drama fans searching for their next superhero fix for a genre that has a library of classics with stories that are more interesting than The Dark Knight to be honest.

If you don't sense the chemistry between Holmes/Gyllenhaal and Bale, that's fair. If you think the romance wasn't fleshed out enough, okay, also a legit gripe. But to then turn around and not understand why he's reacting the way he did is nonsensical. 

Honestly,  comments like "he's a fit young man" and "I didn't see why Batman would stop being Batman" make it sound like you went into this movie with an idea in your head of what Batman is and who Bruce Wayne is and you're evaluating the character based off of how Nolan's Batman conforms to your prior picture of the character rather than evaluating what the movies show you about how THIS Batman/Bruce behaves/thinks/feels/etc.
